evidence: The shipped code was `userEvent.setup({ delay: null, ...options })`, so `setupUser({delay: 0})` genuinely overrides the constant the module's own header calls the thing it exists to enforce; the reviewer's read of the spread order is exactly right. The agent took both halves of the suggestion (reorder the spread and type the parameter `Omit<SetupOptions,'delay'>`), which closes the compile-time and runtime paths together.
guidance_note: When a module's header comment claims it is the single enforcer of a value, check that the signature actually forbids callers from supplying that value before writing the claim.

narrative: One finding, one round of fix, clean second round. The reviewer caught a real gap between a [LAW:single-enforcer] header comment and a type that permitted the bypass, and the agent's fix made the constraint structural rather than defaulted. Nothing here was fix-caused. The PR is the cheap shape: the only defect was the distance between a comment's claim and the type's guarantee.
guidance_observations: The defect class was a comment asserting an invariant the type did not carry - the same class that dominates the rest of this batch.
One review round for a nine-file mechanical migration suggests the diff itself was low-risk; the risk lived entirely in the new helper's signature.

evidence: The diff raised a single `PER_EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS` from 600 to 2500 and that constant is the default for every `exec()` call in the resolver, so the fix for slow `lsof` really did widen the worst case for the fast single-pid `ps` calls too; master now carries `LSOF_EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS` and a separate ps bound, confirming the split was the right shape. The reviewer's suggested per-command timeouts is what the agent implemented.
guidance_note: When widening a shared bound to accommodate one slow caller, first check who else reads that constant - a timeout serving two work shapes is two constants wearing one name.

evidence: The comment the PR added asserted a concrete worst case (`PER_EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS x PEER_LOOKUP_RETRIES (~7.7s)`) while `resolveClientInfo` also runs cache validation, a MAX_PARENT_DEPTH process walk, and readCommand/readCwd - the number was arithmetic over one call site presented as a bound on the whole function. The agent conceded the figure and dropped it rather than recomputing it.
guidance_note: A numeric bound written into a comment is an assertion: derive it from every path the function can take, or state the shape of the bound instead of a number.

evidence: The comment block flagged here was written by d4a9f38, the commit the agent named as the fix for F1; it claims resolver bounds are 'encoded only in lsof/ps exec timeouts and a bounded retry count' while `findLinuxSocketPid` in the same file walks `/proc` with readdir/readlink and no timeout at all (verified in master, src/main/proxy/client-identity.ts:306). The fix replaced one inaccurate comment with another.
guidance_note: When a fix rewrites a comment that makes a completeness claim ('bounds are encoded only in X'), enumerate the function's platform branches before restating the claim.

evidence: The 'no unbounded waits' wording was introduced by d4a9f38 as the fix for F2, and it is false on the Linux path for the same reason as F3 - so the reviewer's comment half is correct and the agent fixed it. The agent declined the AbortSignal half on the ground that README.md line 17 says 'macOS is the primary (and currently only) target' and `/proc` readdir is a kernel FS op, which I verified; declining a speculative bound on a non-target platform is the right call.
guidance_note: Fixing a comment that overstated a bound by writing a differently-worded overstatement of the same bound is the cost of not reading the other platform branch while editing the comment.

narrative: Both round-0 findings were real and both fixes were correct in substance. Round 1 exists entirely because the two comments the round-0 fix wrote each made a fresh completeness claim that the file's Linux branch falsifies - the agent rewrote the prose twice without ever reading `findLinuxSocketPid`. The pushback on adding an AbortSignal to the Linux scan was correct and grounded in a real README boundary. The pattern to take away: this PR paid a whole round for comment prose, not for code.
guidance_observations: Two of the four findings are the agent's own review-fix comments contradicting the code - the fix commit is where comment drift is most likely, not least.
The agent's declines cite project documents (README boundaries, CLAUDE.md) rather than laws when the argument is about scope; that is the right register and it held up on verification.
A file with a platform branch got comments written from one platform's point of view three times in a row; nothing in the process forced the author to open the other branch.

evidence: The comment said 'We don't preventDefault when the user has unrelated focus (chip dropdown, request detail)' while the handler calls `event.preventDefault()` unconditionally once the modifier+F combo matches - the reviewer read both and they disagree. The agent chose the code's behavior as correct (an Electron app has no native Find UI to defer to) and rewrote the comment.
guidance_note: A comment describing a conditional behavior is a claim about a branch; if the code has no such branch, the comment is describing a design that was considered and not built.

evidence: `store/proxy.ts` imported `normalizeQuery`/`recordMatchesSearch` from `components/live-detail/search.ts` while `search.ts` imported `useProxyStore` from `store/proxy.ts` for `useSearchIndex` - a genuine module cycle, and the layering violation (a store importing from a component directory) on top of it. fb24dda extracted the hook into `useSearchIndex.ts` (+70/-0) and stripped 69 lines from search.ts, leaving search.ts pure.
guidance_note: Putting a React hook that reads the store in the same module as the pure projection functions the store imports creates the cycle by construction; split hook from projection when writing the module, not when the bundler complains.

evidence: `normalizeQuery`'s doc said the empty string 'never matches because callers short-circuit on it' while `recordMatchesSearch` returns true for an empty query - two opposite descriptions of the same canonical value in one small module. The agent updated the doc to the match-all semantics the code implements.
guidance_note: When one function's comment describes what a different function does with its return value, verify against that function - the comment is an assertion about code the author is not looking at.

evidence: The 'row dim/dot cues do the narrowing visually' comment is wrong - `visibleRequests` filters non-matching rows out, as the Live tests assert - and the agent confirms it was leftover from an abandoned design. The ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag is a false positive: `gh api repos/promptctl/promptctl/commits/fb24dda` shows the commit touched only search.ts, useSearchIndex.ts and Live.tsx, so this proxy.ts comment is untouched original-PR content the reviewer simply had not read in round 0.
guidance_note: A comment carried forward from a design that was replaced during implementation is dead on arrival; when the behavior changes mid-PR, re-read the comments in the file that described the old behavior.

evidence: `setSearchScope: (scope) => set({ searchScope: scope, selectedRequestId: null })` clears the selection unconditionally, including when the query is empty and scope cannot change `visibleRequests` at all - the reviewer's reading of the store is right. The agent went further than asked and removed the clear entirely, relying on Live.tsx's existing null lookup for out-of-view selections, which is the simpler shape. fb24dda did not touch proxy.ts, so the flag is a false positive and this is original-PR code.
guidance_note: Two sibling setters written together got opposite selection policies with a comment explaining only one of them; decide the policy once for the state, not per setter.

evidence: `appendEvent` rebuilds the requests Map for every SSE frame, so a subscription that sweeps every cached id whenever `state.requests !== prev.requests` really does pay O(cacheSize) per event rather than per eviction. The ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag is a false positive of the relocation kind: fb24dda moved this prune loop out of search.ts into the new useSearchIndex.ts (-69 there, +70 here) with the logic unchanged, so the reviewer is flagging pre-review code it first saw as a new file.

The tooltip said 'within current client/chip filters' while `visibleRequests` in client scope also composes `selectedPromptHash`, and on the All tab there is no single current client - a real if cosmetic mismatch, though the reviewer overstates it as a scoping-logic error rather than copy. The flag is a false positive: 92c06a3 touched only useSearchIndex.ts and proxy.ts, so SearchInput.tsx is untouched original-PR content.
guidance_note: UI copy that enumerates which filters apply is a spec of the filter composition; write it from `visibleRequests` rather than from memory of what the toggle was meant to do.

narrative: Four rounds and seven findings, and not one of them was caused by an earlier fix - every ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag here is a false positive. Rounds 1, 2 and 3 each surfaced original-PR content the reviewer had not read in round 0 (proxy.ts's two setters, the relocated prune loop, SearchInput's tooltip), which means the rounds were bought by reviewer throughput on a 1055-line diff, not by fix quality. Five of the seven findings are prose or policy about code the agent wrote days-cold from an earlier design: three comments contradict the code and one tooltip contradicts the filter pipeline. The agent's fixes were all correct and two improved on the reviewer's suggestion.
guidance_observations: On a diff over 1000 lines the reviewer drip-feeds original-PR findings one round at a time; nothing the agent does to its fixes shortens that, but a self-review pass over the whole diff before opening would.
When a fix extracts a file, the next round re-reviews every line in it as if it were new - expect a round of findings on relocated logic and pre-empt it by reading the moved code before pushing.
Three of seven findings are comments describing an earlier iteration of the design; the cost of implementing against a design doc is comments that describe the doc rather than the code.

evidence: `isSelected={requestId === run.firstIntroducedAt}` genuinely highlights the run's introducer rather than the selected request, so the cyan chip never tracks selection - the reviewer's trace of the consequence (clicking a chip never moves the indicator) follows directly from the expression. The agent threaded `selectedRequestId` down and added a regression test.
guidance_note: When a component takes a `selectedX` prop and renders a selection affordance, the affordance's predicate must reference that prop; a nearby field of the right type is the classic wrong operand.

evidence: The memo key was built from array/string *lengths*, so two different system prompts of equal length under the same request ids produce an identical key and the runs are not recomputed - the exact evolution the tab exists to show would be masked. The agent took the reviewer's second option and depends on the upstream `chain` reference, which Live.tsx already memoizes on selection + lineage.
guidance_note: A change-detection signature built from lengths is not a signature; if a hash of the content is already available in the module, keying on anything cheaper is a collision waiting for a user.

evidence: I read `promptHash.ts` in master: `extractSystem` returns null from every branch that is not a non-empty string or array (`return null` as the fall-through at line 48) and `extractTools` returns null unless `Array.isArray(tools) && tools.length > 0` - neither can return undefined, so the reviewer's premise that `scanRuns` stores undefined is false and the `=== null` checks are correct. Widening to `== null` would have added a guard against a state the producer cannot emit.

narrative: Two real defects in the projection layer and one incorrect reviewer premise, all settled in a single round. The two accepted findings share a root: a component whose props and memo key were wired to plausible-looking neighbours (`firstIntroducedAt` instead of `selectedRequestId`, lengths instead of the hashes the module already computes). The pushback on undefined-vs-null was verified correct against `promptHash.ts` and the agent additionally documented the invariant it was relying on, which is the right way to close a pushback.
guidance_observations: The agent's pushback quoted the upstream function's source in the reply, which is what made it checkable; pushbacks that only cite a law are not.
Both accepted findings would have been caught by asking, of each new prop and each memo key, which value in scope it is actually supposed to name.

evidence: The listener returns early on `!focusIsXtermPane(document.activeElement)` before the engine ever sees the key, so the engine keeps its prefix state while the gate silently drops everything - clicking away mid-chord leaves the badge lit and arms the next keystroke, exactly as described. The agent added a focusout capture that feeds the engine an unbound Escape, using the library's documented prefix-reset contract rather than reaching into its state.
guidance_note: A gate that decides not to deliver an event to a stateful engine owes that engine a cancel; filtering input to a state machine without telling it is how modes get stuck.

evidence: `TmuxCommander.execute` dispatched bare `resize-pane -Z` / `select-pane -U` / `split-window -h` through a proxy that targets tmux's own current pane, while every other input path in the renderer carries an explicit paneId - so a chord could act on a pane other than the one the user focused. The agent confirms the library's KEYMAP.md documents this and fixed it by targeting the UI's selected pane.
guidance_note: When adopting a library's default command table, check whether its commands are implicitly targeted; an untargeted dispatch inside a UI that has an explicit selection is two sources of truth for 'which pane'.

evidence: `const actionTypes: readonly Action["type"][] = [...]` only checks that each listed string is a member of the union; it cannot fail when the union grows, and the accompanying comment claimed 'TypeScript verifies at compile time that every Action variant is enumerated above', which is false. `satisfies Record<Action["type"], true>` is the construct that actually fails to compile on a new variant.
guidance_note: An exhaustiveness test must use a construct that breaks when the union grows - annotating a list with the member type checks the wrong direction, and a hardcoded length pins nothing.

evidence: The finding is against ed9168d, the commit named as F2's fix, which introduced `void proxy.execute('select-pane -t ...')` immediately followed by the binding command - the two-call shape did not exist before that fix. The agent argues the ordering is safe through three layers of implicit guarantees (synchronous pending.push + transport.send, in-order Electron IPC, library FIFO) and then implements the reviewer's own alternative anyway, sending `select-pane -t %X ; <command>` as one write; the concession that the safety proof was implicit is what makes 'partly' the right premise grade.
guidance_note: A fix that adds a second command whose effect the first must precede should encode the ordering in the value (one composed command) rather than in the call sequence - the composed form was available and is also strictly better on tmux's error semantics.

narrative: Three sound round-0 findings - a stuck prefix mode, untargeted tmux commands, and a sham exhaustiveness test with a comment claiming the opposite - all accepted and fixed well. The extra round is bought entirely by F2's fix, which introduced a two-call select-pane-then-command sequence whose ordering rested on unstated assumptions; the agent's round-2 rework collapses it into a single tmux command and is a better answer than either the original fix or the reviewer's chain/await suggestion. Notably the agent argued the reviewer's concern was unfounded and still changed the code, which is the right outcome reached by an awkward route.
guidance_observations: The one avoidable round came from a fix that put an invariant in call order instead of in a value; that is the same failure the PR's own [LAW:dataflow-not-control-flow] comments are about.
The agent's habit of writing comments that assert a compile-time property (here, exhaustiveness) without a construct that enforces it produced one of the three round-0 findings.

evidence: `if (!text || !selectedPaneId) return;` sits above the exact-match branch, so Enter silently does nothing for commands whose target is app/tmux-session/tmux-window, while the suggestions click handler fires the same commands with no pane selected - two entry points to one action with different preconditions. The agent lifted the guard into the sendKeys branch, which is what the reviewer asked for.
guidance_note: When a refactor merges two actions behind one function, re-derive the preconditions per branch; the union of two guards at the top is almost never the right precondition for either.

evidence: The effect called `void window.electronAPI.invoke(...).then(...)` with no rejection handler, so a failing IPC surfaces as an unhandled rejection rather than anything a developer sees. The agent added a `.catch` that logs and preserves the last good snapshot, with a test that drives a rejecting handler.
guidance_note: Every `void`-ed promise at an IPC boundary needs its rejection path decided at the moment it is written; there is no version of this where the default is acceptable.

evidence: The refresh control renders a bare glyph with only a `title`; `title` is not a reliable accessible name, so the button has none. The agent added `aria-label` and a getByRole assertion.
guidance_note: An icon-only control needs its accessible name written at the same time as its glyph - and the same pass should name every other interactive element the diff introduces.

evidence: `return history` hands out the module's live array; `readonly string[]` is erased at runtime, so any consumer can push to it and break the cap and dedupe invariants the module exists to hold. `history.slice()` makes the snapshot real. The law citation fits: the return type was claiming a guarantee the value did not carry.
guidance_note: A `readonly` return type on a module-scoped mutable array documents an intention rather than enforcing it; copy at the boundary of a singleton whose invariants are maintained elsewhere.

evidence: A 50ms real-time wait cannot observe a 5s interval, so the test named 'does not poll on a timer' would pass unchanged if polling came back - it pinned nothing. I checked 1b8a591's patch to ProcessInfoPanel.test.tsx: it added only the IPC-rejection and aria-label tests, so this weak test is original-PR content and the ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag is a false positive. Fake timers advanced 12s is the fix that actually pins the invariant.
guidance_note: A test asserting the absence of a timer must advance a clock past the interval it is ruling out; wall-clock sleeps shorter than the thing being excluded assert nothing.

evidence: `let active = true` is declared inside the effect body, so each run owns its own binding and React runs the previous run's cleanup (`active = false`) before the next effect starts - a late-resolving earlier request therefore checks its own already-false flag and cannot overwrite a newer result. The reviewer's out-of-order-write scenario is not reachable with this code shape, and no request-id ref is needed. The flag is a false positive: 3dfe2e9 touched only the test file, and the `active` pattern is original-PR code.

The disclosure toggle exposes no `aria-expanded`, which is a real gap; it is also the second accessibility gap on the *same two buttons in the same component* - F3's fix in 1b8a591 added an accessible name to the refresh button sitting inches away and did not look at the toggle. The reviewer had to spend a round to say the second half of what it said in round 0.
guidance_note: When a finding names an accessibility property missing on one control, sweep every interactive element the diff adds for the whole accessible-control checklist (name, state, controlled region) in that same fix.

evidence: d8f56bb - the commit named as F7's fix - added `aria-controls="loops-process-info-content"` unconditionally while the element with that id renders only when `expanded && processes && children.length > 0`, so an expanded-but-empty panel points assistive tech at a non-existent element. The fix introduced the dangling reference; the round exists only because of it.
guidance_note: Adding `aria-controls` is a claim that the referenced id exists whenever the attribute does; render the region unconditionally with the attribute, or set the attribute only when the region renders.

evidence: The composer `<textarea>` has only a placeholder, so it has no accessible name - the third accessibility finding in this PR and the third round spent on that one class. d8f56bb touched only ProcessInfoPanel files, so this CommandBar gap is original-PR content that F3's fix could have swept in round 1.
guidance_note: The accessible-name sweep prompted by the first a11y finding must cover the whole diff, not the component the reviewer happened to point at.

evidence: `void submit()` in the keydown handler leaks a rejection when `sendKeys` fails over IPC - identical in shape to F2, which the agent had already fixed in ProcessInfoPanel two rounds earlier without checking the other IPC call sites the same PR added. The agent's own reply says it made the fix 'consistent with the ProcessInfoPanel IPC pattern', naming the sweep it did not do at the time.
guidance_note: When a reviewer flags one unhandled promise at an IPC boundary, grep the diff for every other `void`-ed or floating promise and fix them in the same commit.

evidence: The suggestion-click handler calls `fireCommand(cmd.id)` unawaited and then clears input and records history as if it had succeeded - so it was worse than the submit path F10 fixed one round earlier in the same file, and the agent says so explicitly. Rather than bolting a second try/catch on, it collapsed both call sites onto one `fireAndReset(op, recordText)` helper, which is the better answer to a gap that appeared twice.
guidance_note: Two call sites in one component that perform the same action-then-reset sequence should share the helper before the second one is written; fixing one of a pair by hand guarantees the reviewer finds the other.

narrative: Six rounds on a 783-line diff, and the shape is unmistakable: two defect classes - missing accessible names/state on new controls, and floating promises at IPC boundaries - were each found one instance at a time across four rounds, because every fix addressed exactly the element the reviewer named and swept nothing. F3 to F7 to F8 and F2 to F10 to F11 are both that chain, and F8 is a genuine bug the fix for F7 introduced (an aria-controls pointing at a conditionally-rendered id). The single pushback, on the effect-scoped `active` flag, is technically correct and well argued. Rounds 3 and 4 would not have existed had the round-1 fix swept its own class.
guidance_observations: The dominant cost here is pointwise fixing of an enumerable defect class; the address-pr-reviews loop treats each thread as its own scope and nothing prompts the agent to ask what else in the diff has this property.

The review-fix commits added tests calling `userEvent.setup({ delay: null })` directly, bypassing the `setupUser()` single-enforcer helper that promptctl#12 had introduced four hours earlier the same day - fix commits do not get the same conventions attention as feature commits.
Five of the eleven findings are accessibility or unhandled-rejection nits that a pre-push checklist over the diff would have caught for free; none needed a reviewer to discover.

evidence: The comment asserted that no other editor operation conflicts with an appending writer, while `undo()`, `redo()` and `restoreVersion()` all call `writeFile(activePath(), ...)` and `compressToolResults()` calls `adapter.saveSession([])` - all of which truncate the same live JSONL the guard was added to protect, with data loss as the outcome. This is the highest-severity finding in the batch and the agent accepted it fully, extracting a `liveTailGate` helper and applying it to all five mutators.
guidance_note: Before writing a [LAW:single-enforcer] comment that names the operations which do NOT need the check, enumerate every writer to the resource and verify each one - the comment is a proof obligation, not a summary.

evidence: The `result: SessionSaveResult` prop is declared required and never destructured or read in the body - trivially verifiable from the quoted component. The flag is a false positive: 2a7643e touched editor.ts, editor.test.ts, SessionEditor.tsx and VersionHistoryPanel.tsx, not LiveTailBlockedDialog.tsx, so this is untouched original-PR content. Dropping the prop was right; the banner above the editor already shows the blocking launch.
guidance_note: A prop threaded in anticipation of displaying something, then never displayed, is dead API surface; delete it when the render pass ends without using it.

narrative: One serious finding and one nit, both correct, both cleanly accepted. F1 is the most valuable review catch in the batch: a [LAW:single-enforcer] comment claimed the guard covered the only conflicting operation while four other coordinator mutators truncated the same live file, which would have shipped as silent data loss. The agent's fix generalised properly - a shared gate helper plus renderer-side affordance disabling - and its reply openly says the original framing was wrong. Neither round was caused by a fix; round 1's finding is original-PR content the reviewer had not read.
guidance_observations: The defect and the false claim about it were written in the same comment: the author asserted the enumeration instead of performing it, which is exactly where a reviewer's enumeration pays off.
The agent's fix went past the reported symptom to the class (all five mutators plus the UI affordances), which is why this PR converged in two fix commits where promptctl#21 took five.

evidence: The comment said unknown and already-exited launches both return null, while the handler returns the existing row for an exited launch (`if (launch.status === 'exited') return launch;`) - the doc and the code describe different contracts for the same input. The agent rewrote the comment to enumerate all three return cases.
guidance_note: When a comment enumerates a handler's return cases, derive the list from the returns in the body; a two-case summary of a three-case function is a bug report waiting to be filed.

evidence: A `<div onClick>` row is not focusable and cannot be activated by Enter or Space - a plain keyboard-accessibility defect. The reviewer proposed hand-rolled role/tabIndex/keydown; the agent used a native `<button type="button">` instead, which is the better answer because the semantics come from the element rather than from three attributes that can drift apart.
guidance_note: A clickable row is a button; reach for the native element before reproducing its behaviour with role plus tabIndex plus a key handler.

evidence: `URLSearchParams.get` returns '' rather than null for `?launchId=`, so the `launchId === null` test routes an empty id into the detail view and renders 'Launch not found' where the list belongs - a real reachable bug. The flag is a false positive: 0cc5eac touched launch-handlers.ts and WorkshopLaunchList files only, so Workshop.tsx is untouched original-PR code that round 0 missed.
guidance_note: Parse query params at the URL-to-state boundary into the shape the body wants: `get()` has three outcomes (absent, present-empty, present-valued) and a `=== null` test only covers one.

evidence: 'Workshop' is both the top-tab link text and the page `<h2>`, so `getByText('Workshop', { exact: true })` matches two elements and throws under Playwright strict mode - a real flake source in a smoke test. The role-scoped selector fixes it. The cited law is about changes rippling across a missing seam and has nothing to do with selector specificity; the token is decoration on a correct fix. 1118763 touched only Workshop.tsx and its test, so the e2e spec is original-PR content.
guidance_note: In an app whose nav labels repeat the page headings, every text-based e2e selector is ambiguous by default; scope by role or container when writing the assertion.

evidence: The reviewer asks for imports to support a backwards-compatibility redirect for pre-rename hash URLs; README.md line 9 says in terms 'There is no legacy, no backwards compatibility, no external users to worry about', which I verified, and the canonical external entry point `promptctl://open?...` already routes correctly through the updated TARGET_ROUTE in deep-link.ts. The ask is new scope surfaced on the region 1118763 changed for F3, not a defect in that fix.

This is the same backwards-compatibility redirect request as F5, filed a second time against the same file in the same round, and it is wrong for the same verified reason (README's explicit no-legacy boundary; the deep-link parser already handles the only stable entry point). The reviewer's own phrasing - a redirect gated on sessionId present AND launchId absent-or-empty - is written against the coercion F3's fix had just added, which is what makes it a new-scope finding on the changed region.

`await deps.execute('kill-session -t ...')` throws when tmux has already reaped the session, and the registry flips to exited only after the correlator observes the pane close - so the window between the two is reachable in normal use and a second Stop click lands in it. de76cca touched only the e2e spec, so this is original-PR logic; the fix (match tmux's 'can't find session' reply and treat it as the desired post-state, keep other errors loud) is the right shape.
guidance_note: A terminate path that races an asynchronous observer must treat 'already in the target state' as success; decide that when writing the kill, not when a reviewer describes the race.

evidence: Exited launches are marked exited precisely because their pane went away, so 'Open pane in Loops' on an exited row navigates to a pane id that cannot resolve - a dead end the row's own status data already predicts. de76cca touched only the e2e spec, so this is original-PR content. The agent hid the button behind the same `canTerminate` discriminator the Stop button uses.
guidance_note: Derive every affordance on a status-bearing row from that status when the row is written; an action whose target the status says is gone should not render.

evidence: The file header said the request panel projects off `proxyClientId` while the code matches `clients[*].launchId === launch.launchId` - and the agent's reply explains why the difference matters (one launch produces several client rows as the tool reconnects), so the comment would actively mislead a future change. 3c068eb touched this file for F7/F8 but the header comment is original-PR content.
guidance_note: A file header that names the discriminator each panel projects on is a claim per panel; check each against the code that filters, since these are exactly the lines a later change will trust.

evidence: `launchDetailRoute()` was exported with a [LAW:one-source-of-truth] comment claiming every callsite goes through it, while the row two functions above hard-coded the same `/workshop?launchId=...` string - the helper was written and then not used in its own module. c2e2e7c touched only WorkshopLaunchDetail.tsx, so this is original-PR content.
guidance_note: A helper introduced as the single source for a string shape must be adopted by every existing callsite in the same commit, starting with the ones in its own file; an unused single-source helper is two sources.

evidence: Interpolating a LaunchId straight into a query string is genuinely unsafe construction, but the reviewer's reachability claim is overstated and the agent says why: the har-replayer's synthetic ids are not in the launch registry, so the button that would carry them never renders today. Building the query with URLSearchParams is correct regardless. 4faf74f only added the comment and redirected callers, so the unencoded interpolation is original-PR logic, not something the F10 fix introduced.
guidance_note: Consolidating callsites onto a shared builder is the moment to audit the builder itself - encoding, escaping, empty inputs - because the refactor makes its defects everyone's.

evidence: de76cca, the fix for F4, rewrote this test's comment to say 'The top tab labeled Workshop is active when /workshop is the current route' while changing only the selector - the assertions still prove nothing about the route, and the top tab bar renders everywhere. The fix wrote a stronger claim than the test it was editing could support, which is what the reviewer caught one round later.
guidance_note: When a fix touches a test whose name or comment claims coverage, verify the assertions still support the claim - editing the selector is the moment the claim goes stale.

evidence: The reviewer's stated basis is false: I read `sessionExists` in master (src/main/launch/spawn.ts:195) and it uses the identical `'response' in err` cast with `.response.output.join('\n')` and no `Array.isArray` check, so 'mirror the more defensive extraction used in spawn.ts' asks the agent to copy something that does not exist. The residual theoretical risk is real but sits behind the library's typed contract, so declining and offering a shared probe helper if the contract ever proves shaky is the right call. The finding exists only because F7's fix introduced `isSessionGone`.

narrative: Ten rounds and thirteen findings on a 1719-line diff, and the striking result is that only one round was avoidable by better fixing: F12, where the F4 fix rewrote a test comment into a claim the assertions did not support. Almost every other round is the reviewer surfacing one original-PR finding at a time - the empty-string launchId, the terminate race, the exited-row dead end, the unused route helper, the header comment's wrong discriminator - none of which the agent's fixes caused and all of which a self-review of the diff could have caught. Three pushbacks (two duplicate backwards-compatibility asks, one Array.isArray request premised on a false claim about spawn.ts) were all correct and all verified. The remaining cost is structural: a diff this size gets reviewed a page at a time.
guidance_observations: A 1700-line PR bought ten review rounds mostly through reviewer throughput, not fix quality; splitting the route rename, the new tab, and the terminate IPC would have parallelised the review instead of serialising it.

Two replies cite fabricated commit shas mid-sentence ('fixed in 9a0e... err, next commit', 'commit 3c4f... err, the next commit'), which breaks the address-pr-reviews convention of naming the fix commit and leaves the thread unauditable.

The agent accepts URL-encoding for an admittedly unreachable input here while declining Array.isArray on a typed contract two rounds later; the line between 'correct construction' and 'defending against the impossible' is being drawn per thread rather than from a stated rule.

The reviewer filed the same backwards-compatibility request as two separate threads in one round, and both had to be answered separately - duplicate findings are a real per-round cost the agent absorbs silently.
